scenes.tts: Cargo moves through the Golgi, yet its enzymes stay at their level. How? Chapter one showed the same problem. An E R chaperone drifted forward. A receptor used its K D E L tag to bring it back.
scenes.caption: Cargo moves through the Golgi, yet its enzymes stay at their level. How? Chapter 1 showed the same problem. An ER chaperone drifted forward. A receptor used its KDEL tag to bring it back.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD from chapter 1, unchanged at first: the left-to-right line of BLUE stations inside the rounded BLUE cell outline (rough ER with GREY ribosome dots, three small ERGIC circles, three tall Golgi cisternae, the TGN net, the fork to the door and the shelf), the GREY flow arrow under the line with chevrons drifting right, and the faint TEAL return loop from chapter 1. Colours keep chapter 1's meaning: GOLD = cargo, TEAL = ER chaperone and KDEL, WHITE = receptor, BLUE spiky-coated vesicles = COPI. NEW for this chapter: small ORANGE blocks = early Golgi enzymes, small MAGENTA blocks = late Golgi enzymes. Opening action: GOLD cargo dots immediately stream left to right through the Golgi while ORANGE blocks remain toward cis and MAGENTA blocks remain toward trans. During the first sentence a white question card appears across the top: 'Cargo moves. Enzymes stay. How?' On 'Chapter one' a TEAL chaperone with a 'KDEL' tail replays its trip back along the TEAL loop, held by a WHITE receptor in a COPI vesicle, and settles in the ER; small tag 'chapter 1'.
scenes.narration: Cargo moves through the Golgi, yet its enzymes stay at their level. How? Chapter 1 showed the same problem. An ER chaperone drifted forward. A receptor used its KDEL tag to bring it back.

scenes.visual: Title 'Crossing the Golgi Stack' fades in for 2 s over the top as the camera starts easing in on the three Golgi cisternae; the question card shrinks into the top-left corner and stays small. Flow chevrons keep drifting right.

scenes.tts: Each flattened sac of the stack is a cisterna. The cis face receives cargo arriving from the E R. The trans face passes it on to the trans-Golgi network. Early sugar enzymes are enriched toward cis, later ones toward trans, and they overlap.
scenes.caption: Each flattened sac of the stack is a cisterna. The cis face receives cargo arriving from the ER. The trans face passes it on to the trans-Golgi network. Early sugar enzymes are enriched toward cis, later ones toward trans, and they overlap.
scenes.visual: The Golgi stack now fills about 70% of frame height: three tall BLUE cisternae, the ERGIC circles just off the left edge and the TGN net just off the right edge. On 'cisterna' the middle sac outlines brighter, label 'cisterna'. On 'cis face' the left sac gets label 'cis' and GOLD dots enter it from the left; on 'trans face' the right sac gets label 'trans' and GOLD dots leave it toward the TGN. On 'Early sugar enzymes' ORANGE blocks crowd the cis sac and thin out across the middle; MAGENTA blocks crowd the trans sac and thin out leftward; in the middle sac both colours mix (label 'overlap'). Distribution label: 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Each flattened sac of the stack is a cisterna. The cis face receives cargo arriving from the ER. The trans face passes it on to the trans-Golgi network. Early sugar enzymes are enriched toward cis, later ones toward trans, and they overlap.

scenes.tts: Picture one is the stable-compartment model. Each cisterna is long-lived and keeps a characteristic set of enzymes. Small vesicles bud from one sac and carry cargo forward to the next. The compartments keep their cis, medial, or trans identities as cargo passes through.
scenes.visual: A label 'stable compartments' appears above the stack. The three sacs stay fixed in place (small pin icons at their tops), each holding its ORANGE or MAGENTA blocks without change. Small round vesicles bud from the cis sac carrying GOLD dots, float right and fuse with the middle sac; then again from middle to trans. A short white forward arrow marks each hop. The flow chevrons keep drifting.
scenes.narration: Picture one is the stable-compartment model. Each cisterna is long-lived and keeps a characteristic set of enzymes. Small vesicles bud from one sac and carry cargo forward to the next. The compartments keep their cis, medial, or trans identities as cargo passes through.

scenes.tts: Rothman's lab rebuilt Golgi transport without intact cells. V S V G began in donor Golgi from one cell population. Acceptor Golgi from another population added a sugar after transfer. That sugar was the assay's readout. Transport needed A T P and cytosol.
scenes.caption: Rothman's lab rebuilt Golgi transport without intact cells. VSV G began in donor Golgi from one cell population. Acceptor Golgi from another population added a sugar after transfer. That sugar was the assay's readout. Transport needed ATP and cytosol.
scenes.visual: The cell fades back; the stack is lifted into a large test tube drawn as a simple outline, label 'cell-free system'. A second, separate stack drops in beside it: left stack label 'donor', right stack label 'acceptor'. GOLD cargo dots labelled 'VSV G' appear only in the donor stack. On 'added a sugar after transfer', a DASHED arrow appears between the stacks, labelled 'transfer inferred', and a separate assay card changes from 'no added sugar' to 'added sugar detected'; no cargo dot is shown crossing the gap. On 'A T P and cytosol' two small icons drop into the tube, a lightning-bolt chip 'ATP' and a cloudy wash 'cytosol'; the positive assay card appears only while both are present. Small caption 'Rothman laboratory'.
scenes.narration: Rothman's lab rebuilt Golgi transport without intact cells. VSV G began in donor Golgi from one cell population. Acceptor Golgi from another population added a sugar after transfer. That sugar was the assay's readout. Transport needed ATP and cytosol.

scenes.tts: Now weigh what the assay showed. Does it prove vesicles carry cargo forward, sac by sac, inside one stack? Separate what the experiment measured from the mechanism its inventors proposed.
scenes.visual: A white question card across the top: 'Proof of within-stack vesicle transport?' The two stacks in the tube stay; a magnifier icon hovers over the gap between them.
scenes.narration: Now weigh what the assay showed. Does it prove vesicles carry cargo forward, sac by sac, inside one stack? Separate what the experiment measured from the mechanism its inventors proposed.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card stays. Near-stillness by design: the GOLD dots drift slowly in the liquid between the two stacks, the ATP chip glows gently, the magnifier bobs.

scenes.tts: Not on its own. The assay inferred transfer between separate Golgi populations from the sugar readout. It did not watch cargo move within one stack. Nor did it identify the carrier that crossed between populations. And transfer between populations fits the second picture too.
scenes.visual: The question card dissolves. A white bracket spans the gap between the two stacks, label 'inferred: between populations'. A dashed white bracket inside the donor stack, across its own sacs, gets label 'not seen: within one stack' and a small white '?'. On 'identify the carrier' a carrier outline with a question mark appears over the gap. On 'the second picture' the tube fades and the cell world returns with the stack centred, ready for the next model.
scenes.narration: Not on its own. The assay inferred transfer between separate Golgi populations from the sugar readout. It did not watch cargo move within one stack. Nor did it identify the carrier that crossed between populations. And transfer between populations fits the second picture too.

scenes.tts: Picture two is the cisternal maturation model. Here the cisterna itself carries the cargo. It forms at the cis face with cargo inside. Then it moves through the stack and ends as trans Golgi and trans-Golgi network. The compartment changes identity while its cargo remains inside.
scenes.visual: Label 'cisternal maturation' replaces 'stable compartments'; the pin icons vanish. A new sac forms at the cis face from small arriving ERGIC carriers, with GOLD cargo dots inside it and ORANGE blocks in its membrane. On 'moves through the stack' this one sac slides slowly rightward, pushing its neighbours along; a new sac forms behind it at cis. As it travels, the GOLD cargo stays inside it the whole way. On 'ends as trans Golgi' it reaches the trans position and on 'trans-Golgi network' it frays into the tubular TGN net, releasing its GOLD dots toward the fork.
scenes.narration: Picture two is the cisternal maturation model. Here the cisterna itself carries the cargo. It forms at the cis face with cargo inside. Then it moves through the stack and ends as trans Golgi and trans-Golgi network. The compartment changes identity while its cargo remains inside.

scenes.tts: So how do the enzymes stay at their level? They keep being carried backward, in COPI vesicles, to the younger cisterna behind. Backward recycling replaces early enzymes with later ones as each cisterna matures. The sacs flow forward, while the enzymes keep going back.
scenes.caption: So how do the enzymes stay at their level? They keep being carried backward, in COPI vesicles, to the younger cisterna behind. The sacs flow forward, while the enzymes keep going back.
scenes.visual: Replay the moving sac at half speed. As it moves right, BLUE spiky-coated vesicles labelled 'COPI' bud from it carrying ORANGE blocks and travel LEFT, against the flow chevrons, into the younger sac behind it. As it nears trans, MAGENTA blocks arrive in it from the older sac ahead, so it gains MAGENTA as it loses ORANGE. A thin ORANGE return arrow loops leftward under the stack and stays. The net picture: sacs drift right, ORANGE blocks keep hopping left, and the ORANGE zone stays at the cis end throughout.
scenes.narration: So how do the enzymes stay at their level? They keep being carried backward, in COPI vesicles, to the younger cisterna behind. The sacs flow forward, while the enzymes keep going back.

scenes.tts: That is the K D E L retrieval logic: recycling against the flow. The comparison is only the logic. Golgi enzymes use different retention and retrieval machinery, not the K D E L receptor.
scenes.caption: That is the KDEL retrieval logic: recycling against the flow. The comparison is only the logic. Golgi enzymes use different retention and retrieval machinery, not the KDEL receptor.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back a little so the faint TEAL return loop from chapter 1 (ERGIC and Golgi back to ER) is visible above the ORANGE return arrow under the stack. On 'recycling against the flow' both loops brighten together and a white label between them reads 'recycling against the flow'. On 'their own' the ORANGE loop gets a small separate label 'own machinery', and the TEAL loop dims back to faint.
scenes.narration: That is the KDEL retrieval logic: recycling against the flow. The comparison is only the logic. Golgi enzymes use different retention and retrieval machinery, not the KDEL receptor.

scenes.tts: Put the two pictures side by side. In one, the sacs stay put and the cargo hops between them. In the other, the cargo stays inside a sac that changes character from cis to trans.
scenes.visual: Split screen, two copies of the stack side by side, each filling most of the frame height. Left, label 'stable compartments': pinned sacs with fixed ORANGE and MAGENTA blocks, GOLD cargo hopping right in small vesicles. Right, label 'cisternal maturation': one sac with GOLD cargo inside sliding right while its blocks change from ORANGE to MAGENTA, COPI vesicles carrying ORANGE back left. Both run in a slow loop. Corner label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Put the two pictures side by side. In one, the sacs stay put and the cargo hops between them. In the other, the cargo stays inside a sac that changes character from cis to trans.

scenes.tts: Which is right? In the text, predict how fast one filmed cisterna should change. For stacked mammalian Golgi, the question remains open. Glick and Luini judged that no single model explains every observation. They proposed maturation as the best candidate for a shared core.
scenes.visual: The split screen stays, both loops still running. On 'Which is right?' a white '?' sits between the two panels. On 'one filmed cisterna' a small camera icon hovers over the right panel with a white tag 'predict timing in the text', and no timing or result is shown. On 'stacked mammalian Golgi' both panels gain a small label 'mammalian stack: open'. On 'no single model' a thin white outline draws around both panels together; on 'best candidate for a shared core' the right panel brightens slightly, label 'proposed shared core', while the left panel stays fully visible, not crossed out. Small caption 'Glick & Luini'.
scenes.narration: Which is right? In the text, predict how fast one filmed cisterna should change. For stacked mammalian Golgi, the question remains open. Glick and Luini judged that no single model explains every observation. They proposed maturation as the best candidate for a shared core.

scenes.tts: So how does cargo cross the stack while its enzymes stay put? Fixed sacs and moving vesicles, or moving sacs and recycled enzymes. Either way, the cargo goes forward.
scenes.visual: Zoom back out to the whole cell world of chapter 1. The question from the opening returns faintly at the top. The Golgi stack alternates gently between the two pictures (pinned sacs with hopping vesicles, then a sliding sac with ORANGE blocks returning). On 'the cargo goes forward' the GREY flow chevrons brighten and a GOLD stream runs on through the TGN to the fork. The question fades as the answer finishes.
scenes.narration: So how does cargo cross the stack while its enzymes stay put? Fixed sacs and moving vesicles, or moving sacs and recycled enzymes. Either way, the cargo goes forward.

scenes.line: Fixed sacs and moving vesicles, or moving sacs and recycled enzymes.
scenes.visual: End card: 'Fixed sacs and moving vesicles, or moving sacs and recycled enzymes.' over the softly drifting world.
